story.heading: Everything in one place, before you need it
paragraphs: When something goes wrong, such as a power cut, a storm, a sudden hospital visit or a quick evacuation, the information you need is often scattered across phones, drawers and memories. This binder gathers it into one place, so you, or anyone helping you, can find it in seconds.
Fill it in on screen and save it, or print the blank pages and write by hand. Every field is a clear box or line, margins are safe for home printers, and the pages read well in black and white.

It is written for households in any country. You add your own local emergency number, water amounts appear in both liters and US gallons, and there is a cross-border section for families with papers, property or relatives in more than one country.

story.heading: A tracker that keeps it current
paragraphs: A binder is only useful if it is up to date. The companion spreadsheet lists your stored supplies and your documents (passports, ID cards, residence permits, insurance policies, vehicle papers) with their expiry dates. Each row shows the days left and a clear status: OK, Expires soon, Expired or No date.
A dashboard counts what needs attention, a calculator works out water and food targets for your household, and a review tab tells you when your next six-month check is due.
story.note_html: Private by design. The binder records where things are and who to call. It never asks for passwords, PINs, full account or card numbers, document numbers or crypto seed phrases.

story.heading: Decide once a week, not every evening
paragraphs: The question "what's for dinner?" is easier to answer on a quiet Sunday than at six o'clock on a busy Tuesday. This planner turns it into a short weekly routine: check what you already have, choose the week's meals, write one grocery list, and shop once.

Start by filling in a few setup pages: who you cook for and what they love or avoid, which nights are busy, a handful of theme nights, and a bank of go-to meals your household already enjoys. After that, planning a week is mostly picking from your own list.

Every weekly plan has space for breakfast, lunch, dinner and snacks, a busy-night tick for each day, and boxes for what to prep ahead, what to use up first and how to handle leftovers. The facing grocery list is grouped by store section, so you walk each aisle once.

story.heading: A spreadsheet that writes the grocery list

story.note_html: Made for any kitchen. Units are flexible, a conversions page covers cups, grams, ounces and oven temperatures in Celsius, Fahrenheit and gas marks, and nothing assumes a particular country, store or diet.

story.heading: A few goals, with a real plan behind each one
paragraphs: A fresh year makes it tempting to write a long list of resolutions and hope for the best. This planner takes a calmer route: look back first, choose a small number of goals that genuinely matter to you, and give each one a plan you can start this week.

It opens with a year review and a check-in on eight areas of life, so you can see where a small change would help most. Then you pick a word for the year, list up to eight goals, and turn the important ones into goal action plans: what done looks like, why it matters, milestones with dates, the first three steps, and what you will do if something gets in the way.
A year-by-quarter page spreads the milestones across four seasons, and monthly and weekly pages keep the next step in front of you without turning the year into one giant to-do list.

story.heading: Habits you can actually keep, and a spreadsheet that keeps count
paragraphs: Goals move forward through small, repeated actions. The habit builder helps you design a habit before you start it, with a cue, a tiny first version and a way to track it. Then tick boxes on the monthly tracker for up to twelve habits, fill a whole year of one habit on the year-in-habits grid, or take on a 100-day challenge.

Weekly, monthly and quarterly reviews and a mid-year reset help you adjust without starting over. The companion spreadsheet works in Microsoft Excel and Google Sheets: list goals and milestones, tick daily habits, and goal progress, habit totals by month and a one-screen dashboard update by themselves.
story.note_html: Undated, so it starts when you do. Begin in January, on a birthday or on any Monday. The planner never tells you what your goals should be; it simply helps you follow through on the ones you choose.

story.heading: The whole gathering, on paper before the doorbell rings
paragraphs: Replies scattered across texts, a menu in your head, one oven and five dishes that all need it at four o'clock, and a cousin who mentioned an allergy you cannot quite remember. This planner puts a holiday gathering in one place: who is coming, what they can eat, what you are serving, what to buy, and what needs doing when.

Start with an event overview and a guest list with RSVPs and party sizes. A dietary needs tracker keeps what each guest has told you next to the dishes that suit them. Plan the menu course by course, decide who is bringing what, copy recipes onto fillable recipe cards, and turn it all into a grocery list sorted by store aisle.

A prep countdown runs from two weeks out to the night before, then an hour-by-hour plan and an oven and stovetop schedule carry you through the day. There is a seating plan with a name box for every seat, a place-setting check, a house-prep checklist, overnight-guest pages with a house-info card, a drinks planner with alcohol-free options, and a helpers-and-jobs list. Afterwards, log leftovers, track thank-you notes and write down what to keep for next year. A season-at-a-glance page covers Thanksgiving through New Year's Day. Every page is fillable on screen and prints cleanly in Letter or A4.

story.heading: A spreadsheet that keeps the gathering on track
paragraphs: On Setup, enter the date, the time the meal is served and when guests arrive. The Guests tab tracks invitations, RSVPs, party sizes, kids, dietary needs, what each guest is bringing and who is staying over; confirmed headcount is added up for you.

The Countdown tab holds a starter list of hosting jobs, each set a number of days before the event; due dates are worked out and overdue or due-soon jobs are highlighted. The Cooking Schedule works out when each dish should start from its cooking and resting minutes and the time you want it ready. The Grocery List sorts items by aisle and totals what is still to buy, and the Leftovers tab shows a use-by date from the number of days you choose.
The Dashboard shows days to go, confirmed guests, dietary needs, overnight guests, menu coverage by course, countdown progress, groceries left to buy and the first oven start time.
Rows marked “(example)” show how it works; type over them or clear them.
story.note_html: A planning tool, not professional advice. It does not give medical, nutrition or food-safety advice. Always confirm allergies and dietary needs directly with each guest, read ingredient labels, and follow your own recipes and official food-safety guidance for cooking times, temperatures and storing leftovers. Keep door codes and passwords out of the files.

story.heading: A season on paper, counted from your own frost dates
paragraphs: Seed packets in a drawer, a half-remembered last-frost date, and a sketch of the beds that never quite matches what went in. This planner puts a growing season in one place: what you want to grow, when to sow from dates you choose, where each crop goes, and what you actually harvested.

Start with a garden overview and a frost-dates page you fill in yourself. There is no built-in zone, country calendar or map. Look up local frost dates or a hardiness zone from your national weather or agriculture service (for example, USDA in the United States), then adjust them for your own garden. The same pages work in both hemispheres.

List the seed you already have, plan sowings month by month, and sketch each bed on a square-foot grid or a row layout. A four-year rotation page is there as a record, so related crops can move next season if you want them to. Keep planting, watering and harvest logs, take a weekly walk around the plot, and close the season with a review, notes on seed to save, and a page for next year. Every page is fillable on screen and prints cleanly in Letter or A4.

story.heading: A spreadsheet that works out the sowing dates
paragraphs: On Setup, enter a garden name, the season, your last spring frost, your first autumn frost, and the units you use. If autumn falls in the next calendar year, use that later date. Days until each frost and the length of the frost-free stretch are calculated for you.

The Sowing Calendar takes the week offsets you type — weeks before last frost to start indoors, weeks after to transplant or direct-sow, and weeks before first autumn frost for a late crop — and turns them into dates. A seed inventory flags packets that are past their sow-by date or due within 30 days. The Bed Planner calculates area from the width and length you enter. The Harvest Tracker totals each crop and drives a chart. Garden Costs is a small log of seeds, soil, tools and supplies only, not a household budget.
The Dashboard shows days until each frost date, seeds expiring, tasks in the next 14 days, harvest totals and garden spend.
Rows marked “(example)” show how it works; they are not a planting calendar for your climate. Type over them or clear them.
story.note_html: A planning and record-keeping tool, not gardening advice. It does not recommend pesticides, herbicides or other chemical treatments, and it does not promise a yield. Sowing dates depend on your climate, your site and the guidance on your seed packet. If you need advice, ask a qualified local professional or your agricultural extension or advisory service.
